summary: Investigation is inconclusive. The leading hypothesis—that the portfolio-service database pool reduction caused connection starvation—has only 45% confidence and is not fully supported by the verified data. Key observations show simultaneous latency spikes in both api-gateway and portfolio-service starting before the config change, and critical resource utilization metrics are missing. Immediate mitigation and targeted data collection are required to discriminate between the remaining hypotheses.

ranked_hypotheses.title: Portfolio-service DB pool reduction caused connection starvation
ranked_hypotheses.statement: A configuration change at 2026-03-10T09:52:00Z reduced the portfolio-service database pool max size from 50 to 5, starving connections to the shared ledger‑db. This caused portfolio-service latency spikes, which propagated to api‑gateway latency and resulted in 504 upstream timeouts for the /v1/portfolio/* endpoint.

causal_chain.claim: Config change reduced DB pool size
Reduced pool caused connection starvation on ledger‑db
Increased latency in portfolio-service caused api‑gateway latency spikes
Gateway latency spikes produced 504 upstream timeouts

assumptions: DB connection starvation directly translates to observed latency spikes in portfolio-service

ranked_hypotheses.title: Gateway HTTP/2 upgrade introduced resource pressure
ranked_hypotheses.statement: The api‑gateway upgrade to version v9.3.0 at 2026-03-10T08:00:00Z enabled HTTP/2 to upstreams, increasing connection handling overhead and exhausting gateway resources, which manifested as latency spikes and 504 timeouts for the portfolio endpoint.

causal_chain.claim: HTTP/2 increased connection/resource usage beyond capacity
Resource pressure caused gateway latency spikes
Latency spikes led to upstream 504 errors

assumptions: HTTP/2 upgrade materially increased connection count or processing load on the gateway
No other concurrent changes explain the latency

ranked_hypotheses.title: Shared ledger‑db overload degraded portfolio-service
ranked_hypotheses.statement: The shared ledger‑db (PostgreSQL) became overloaded due to concurrent load from multiple services, causing high query latency for portfolio-service, which then propagated to api‑gateway resulting in timeouts.

causal_chain.claim: Portfolio latency caused gateway latency spikes

assumptions: Ledger‑db overload directly translates to observed latency in portfolio-service
Shared nature of ledger‑db leads to contention

ranked_hypotheses.title: Load balancer/network issue affecting portfolio traffic
ranked_hypotheses.statement: A change or failure in the load balancer or network path for the /v1/portfolio/* endpoint introduced additional latency and packet loss, causing api‑gateway timeouts.

causal_chain.claim: Increased latency manifested as gateway latency spikes
Latency spikes resulted in 504 upstream errors

assumptions: No other network changes were made; the observed latency is attributable to LB/network

facts.statement: A configuration change reduced the portfolio-service database pool max size from 50 to 5 at 2026-03-10T09:52:00Z.
api-gateway p99 latency spiked to ~1850 ms (avg) and up to 4418 ms (max) starting at 2026-03-10T09:50:00Z.
api-gateway error rate jumped to >1 % (avg 1.66 %) and max 7.18 % starting at 2026-03-10T09:50:00Z.
First 504 WARN log for the portfolio endpoint was recorded at 2026-03-10T09:53:53Z.
portfolio-service p99 latency spiked to ~1865 ms (avg) and up to 4546 ms (max) starting at 2026-03-10T09:50:00Z.
Elevated latency and 504 errors are concentrated on the endpoint GET /v1/portfolio/holdings routed to upstream service portfolio-service.
api-gateway calls portfolio-service via HTTP for the /v1/portfolio/* endpoint.
Portfolio-service accesses three downstream components: ledger-db (shared PostgreSQL), market-data-service (HTTP), and redis-cache (shared Redis).

assumptions: DB connection starvation directly translates to the observed latency spikes in portfolio-service.
The HTTP/2 upgrade materially increased connection count or processing load on the gateway, leading to resource pressure.
Ledger‑db overload directly translates to the observed latency in portfolio-service.
No other network or load‑balancer changes were made that could explain the latency.

timeline.event: api-gateway upgraded to version v9.3.0 with HTTP/2 enabled (unverified deployment).
Simultaneous latency spikes begin in api-gateway (p99 ~1850 ms) and portfolio-service (p99 ~1865 ms).
Configuration change reduces portfolio-service DB pool max size from 50 to 5.
First 504 warning logged for portfolio endpoint (upstream timeout).

recommended_actions.action: Revert the portfolio-service database pool max size back to its prior value (50) and monitor latency.
recommended_actions.rationale: If connection starvation is the cause, restoring pool capacity should alleviate latency; this change is low‑risk and can be rolled back quickly.

recommended_actions.action: Temporarily disable HTTP/2 on api-gateway (rollback to previous envoy filter configuration) and observe if latency improves.
recommended_actions.rationale: If the HTTP/2 upgrade introduced resource pressure, disabling it provides a quick mitigation while data is collected.

recommended_actions.action: Collect missing resource utilization metrics for api-gateway (CPU, memory, active connections, thread‑pool usage) for the window 08:00‑10:30 UTC.
recommended_actions.rationale: These metrics are required to confirm or refute hypothesis H2 regarding gateway resource saturation.

recommended_actions.action: Gather portfolio-service DB pool metrics (active connections, wait queue length, acquisition latency) before and after the 09:52 change.
recommended_actions.rationale: Direct evidence of connection starvation will validate or invalidate hypothesis H1.

recommended_actions.action: Obtain ledger‑db performance metrics (CPU, active connections, query latency, timeout logs) for 09:30‑10:30 UTC.
recommended_actions.rationale: Needed to assess hypothesis H3 that shared ledger‑db overload contributed to the incident.

recommended_actions.action: Review load‑balancer configuration change logs and network path health for the /v1/portfolio/* endpoint.
recommended_actions.rationale: To evaluate hypothesis H4 concerning possible LB/network issues.

recommended_actions.action: Implement alerting on portfolio-service DB pool usage and api-gateway resource saturation thresholds.
recommended_actions.rationale: Pre‑emptively detect similar conditions in the future.

recommended_actions.action: Establish a post‑mortem process to verify all dependency flags (e.g., shared resources) and ensure they are documented and observable.
recommended_actions.rationale: Reduces uncertainty from unverified assumptions like the shared nature of ledger‑db and redis‑cache.

data_gaps: Missing api-gateway resource utilization metrics (CPU %, memory %, active connection count, thread‑pool usage) for the incident window.
No portfolio-service database pool usage metrics (active connections, wait queue length, acquisition latency) around the 09:52 config change.
Ledger‑db performance metrics (CPU, connections, query latency) are unavailable for the relevant period.
Verification of the 'shared' flag for ledger‑db and redis‑cache is unverified.
Load‑balancer change logs and network latency measurements for the portfolio endpoint are absent.
what_would_change_the_conclusion: Evidence of active connection starvation in portfolio-service after the DB pool reduction (e.g., high wait queue length, increased acquisition latency).
Metrics showing api-gateway CPU, memory, or connection saturation coinciding with the latency spike, confirming resource pressure from the HTTP/2 upgrade.
Ledger‑db load metrics indicating overload (high CPU, connection count, query latency) during the incident window.
Logs or change records indicating a load‑balancer or network configuration change affecting the /v1/portfolio/* path.
